content: Certainly. Clinical and Epidemiological Features of Aeromonas spp. Aeromonas species are Gram-negative, non-spore-forming, facultative anaerobic bacilli belonging to the Vibrionaceae family. They share many similarities with the Enterobacteriaceae family. The genus is divided into two groups: psychrophilic non-motile aeromonads, which include A. salmonicida, an obligate fish pathogen, and mesophilic motile aeromonads, which are of potential human health significance. The latter group includes species such as A. hydrophila, A. caviae, A. veronii subspecies sobria, A. jandaei, A. veronii subspecies veronii, and A. schubertii. These bacteria are commonly found in freshwater environments, soil, and various foods, particularly meat and milk. Human Health Effects Aeromonas spp. can cause infections in humans, including septicemia, particularly in immunocompromised patients, as well as wound infections and respiratory tract infections. While there have been claims that Aeromonas spp. can cause gastrointestinal illness, epidemiological evidence remains inconsistent. Despite their ability to produce toxins in vitro, diarrhea has not been reliably induced in test animals or human volunteers. Source and Occurrence Aeromonas spp. are widespread in water, soil, and food, especially meat, fish, and milk. They are commonly detected in most freshwater sources and have been found in treated drinking water supplies, often due to regrowth in distribution systems. Factors influencing their presence in water systems include organic content, temperature, water residence time, and residual chlorine levels. Routes of Exposure Wound infections have been linked to activities involving contaminated soil and water, such as swimming, diving, boating, and fishing. Septicemia can result from such wound infections. In immunocompromised individuals, septicemia may also arise from Aeromonas spp. present in their gastrointestinal tract. Significance in Drinking Water Although Aeromonas spp. are frequently isolated from drinking water, there is limited evidence to support waterborne transmission. Aeromonads found in drinking water typically do not belong to the same DNA homology groups as those associated with gastroenteritis cases. Their presence in drinking water is generally considered a nuisance rather than a significant health risk. Proper disinfection and control measures, such as optimizing organic carbon removal, reducing water residence time, and maintaining disinfectant residuals, can minimize their growth in distribution systems. Clinical and Epidemiological Features of Burkholderia pseudomallei Burkholderia pseudomallei is a Gram-negative bacillus commonly found in soil and muddy water, predominantly in tropical regions such as northern Australia and Southeast Asia. The organism is acid-tolerant and can survive in water for extended periods without nutrients. Human Health Effects Burkholderia pseudomallei causes melioidosis, a disease endemic to northern Australia and other tropical regions. The most common clinical manifestation is pneumonia, which can be fatal. In some areas, melioidosis is the leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia. Cases occur year-round but peak during the rainy season. Patients may present with milder forms of pneumonia that respond well to antibiotics, or with severe septicemic pneumonia. Other symptoms include skin abscesses or ulcers, abscesses in internal organs, and rare neurological illnesses such as brainstem encephalitis and acute paraplegia. While melioidosis can occur in healthy individuals, it primarily affects those with impaired immune defenses due to underlying conditions, poor nutrition, or suboptimal living conditions. Source and Occurrence The organism is predominantly found in tropical soils and surface-accumulated muddy water, from where it can contaminate raw water sources and drinking water supplies. The infectious dose in drinking water that constitutes a significant risk is not known. Routes of Exposure Most infections occur through contact of skin cuts or abrasions with contaminated water. In Southeast Asia, rice paddies are a significant source of infection. Other routes of infection include inhalation and ingestion, though their relative importance is unclear. Significance in Drinking Water In two Australian outbreaks of melioidosis, indistinguishable isolates of B. pseudomallei were cultured from both patients and the drinking water supply. One outbreak was linked to chlorination failure and pipe replacement, while the other involved an unchlorinated water supply. Effective control measures within a water safety plan include established treatment and disinfection processes for drinking water, as well as protecting the distribution system from contamination during repairs and maintenance. Heterotrophic plate counts (HPC) and disinfectant residuals can be used to monitor water treatment effectiveness and indicate protection against B. pseudomallei. However, due to its environmental occurrence, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are not suitable indicators for the presence of this organism. Clinical and Epidemiological Features of Campylobacter spp. Campylobacter species are microaerophilic (requiring reduced oxygen) and capnophilic (requiring increased carbon dioxide) Gram-negative, curved spiral rods with a single unsheathed polar flagellum. They are among the most important causes of acute gastroenteritis worldwide. Campylobacter jejuni is the most frequently isolated species from patients with acute diarrheal disease, while C. coli, C. lari, and C. fetus are less commonly implicated. Human Health Effects An important feature of C. jejuni is its relatively high infectivity, with as few as 1,000 organisms capable of causing infection. Most symptomatic infections occur in infancy and early childhood, with an incubation period of 2–4 days. Clinical symptoms include abdominal pain, diarrhea (with or without blood or fecal leukocytes), vomiting, chills, and fever. The infection is self-limiting and typically resolves within 3–7 days, though relapses may occur in 5–10% of untreated patients. Other clinical manifestations include reactive arthritis and meningitis. C. jejuni infection has also been associated with Guillain-Barré syndrome, an acute demyelinating disease of the peripheral nerves. Source and Occurrence Campylobacter spp. are found in various environments. Wild and domestic animals, especially poultry, wild birds, and cattle, are important reservoirs. Pets and other animals may also serve as reservoirs. Food, including meat and unpasteurized milk, is a significant source of Campylobacter infections. Water is another important source, with the occurrence of the organisms in surface waters strongly influenced by rainfall, water temperature, and the presence of waterfowl. Routes of Exposure Most Campylobacter infections are sporadic, with food being a common source. Transmission to humans typically occurs through the consumption of animal products, particularly poultry and unpasteurized milk. Contaminated drinking water supplies have been identified as a source of outbreaks, with cases ranging from a few to several thousand. Sources include inadequately chlorinated surface water supplies and fecal contamination of water storage reservoirs by wild birds. Significance in Drinking Water Contaminated drinking water supplies are a significant source of Campylobacteriosis outbreaks. Waterborne transmission has been confirmed by isolating the same strains from patients and the drinking water they consumed. Control measures within a water safety plan include protecting raw water supplies from human and animal waste, adequate treatment, and protecting water during distribution. Treated and disinfected water storage should be protected from bird feces. Campylobacter spp. are fecally borne pathogens and are not particularly resistant to disinfection. Therefore, E. coli or thermotolerant coliforms are appropriate indicators for the presence or absence of Campylobacter spp. in drinking water supplies.
